content: Blood lead level (BLL) is a measurement of the concentration of lead present in the body. A level of 48 micromoles per liter (µmol/L) is considered significant. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a BLL of 10 micrograms per deciliter (µg/dL) or higher is regarded as a cause for concern. However, it is important to note that lead exposure can negatively affect development even at BLLs below 10 µg/dL. In Australia, the acceptable threshold for lead in blood was reduced from 25 µg/dL to 10 µg/dL in 1992. Subsequently, in 1993, the National Health and Medical Research Council (NH&MRC) established a national target to be achieved by 1998. This target aimed for all Australians, except those working in lead-related industries, to have a BLL of less than 15 µg/dL. Specific strategies were implemented to ensure that 90% of pre-school-aged children would have BLLs below 15 µg/dL. Despite these efforts, 7% of individuals were found to have BLLs exceeding 15 µg/dL.
